title: Money Mastery
tagline: Read a paycheck, budget, build credit, dodge scams and start investing.
description: Learn to read your paycheck, stop worrying about taxes, and set up a budget, a bank account and an emergency fund that actually work. Build credit safely, use a credit card without falling into debt, spot scams and bad loans, and start investing the simple way.

units.title: Paychecks and Taxes
units.description: Know where your paycheck goes and why taxes are less scary than they look.

levels.title: Read Your Paycheck
levels.summary: Gross pay, take-home pay and the lines on your pay stub.

steps.title: Gross pay vs take-home pay
steps.body:
**Gross pay** is what you earned before anything is taken out. Work 20 hours at $16/hour and your gross pay is $320.

**Take-home pay** (also called **net pay**) is what actually lands in your bank account after taxes and other deductions.

> Always plan your spending with take-home pay. A $16/hour job does not put $16/hour in your pocket.
steps.tip: Find your last pay stub and circle two numbers: gross pay and net pay. Net pay is the number your budget is built on.

steps.prompt: You get your first paycheck. Which number should you use to plan your spending?
options: Gross pay
Net (take-home) pay
Your hourly rate times 40 hours
Year-to-date gross pay
feedback: Gross pay includes money that goes to taxes before you ever see it.
Right. Net pay is the money you can actually spend.
That ignores taxes, and many first jobs are not 40 hours a week.
Year-to-date is the total for the whole year so far, not one check.
steps.explain: Net pay is what reaches your account. Budgeting with gross pay makes you think you have more money than you do.

steps.title: What gets taken out
steps.body:
Common lines on a pay stub:
- **Federal income tax**: the main tax, held back for the IRS.
- **State income tax**: some states have none.
- **Social Security and Medicare** (often labeled **FICA**): 6.2% + 1.45% = **7.65%** of pay for most workers.
- **Benefits** you chose, like health insurance or a 401(k) (a retirement savings account through work).

How much you keep depends on your pay, your state and your benefits. On a small part-time check, most of it usually reaches you.
steps.tip: Read every pay stub for one minute: check your hours and pay rate. Payroll mistakes happen, and you only catch them if you look.

source.label: IRS: Topic 751, Social Security and Medicare tax rates

steps.prompt: Your paycheck is $1,000 gross. About 20% goes to taxes and deductions. About how much do you take home?
steps.hint: Find 20% of $1,000 first, then subtract it from $1,000. Or just find 80%, the part you keep.

steps.prompt: Match each pay stub term to what it means.
pairs: What actually reaches your bank account
steps.explain: These four terms appear on almost every pay stub. YTD is handy at tax time and for checking you were paid for every shift.

steps.title: The W-4 form
steps.body:
On your first day you fill out a **W-4**. It tells your employer how much federal income tax to hold back from each check.

If you are single with one job, you usually just fill in your name and filing status and sign it.

Holding back tax is like **prepaying**. If too much was held back, you get a **refund** in the spring. If too little, you owe.
steps.tip: If you work two jobs at once, use the free IRS Tax Withholding Estimator on irs.gov before you fill out the second W-4, so you do not owe a surprise bill in April.

steps.prompt: A coworker says: "Write EXEMPT on your W-4. Then no tax comes out and your checks are bigger." What do you do?

options.text: Fill it out normally. Exempt is only for people who owe no federal income tax at all for the year.
options.feedback: Right. If you claim exempt and do owe tax, you get a bill (and maybe a penalty) later.

options.text: Write exempt. Bigger checks now are always better.
options.feedback: The tax is still due. You just pay it all at once next spring instead of a little each check.

options.text: Skip the W-4 so nothing is withheld.
options.feedback: Without a W-4, your employer still withholds, using default settings. Skipping it does not stop withholding.

steps.hint: Withholding is prepaying a tax you will owe anyway. What happens if you prepay nothing?
steps.explain: Withholding does not change how much tax you owe. It only changes when you pay it. Fill out the W-4 honestly.

steps.prompt: A big tax refund means you got free money from the government.
steps.explain: A refund is your own money coming back. Too much was held from your paychecks during the year, and the IRS returns the extra.

steps.prompt: Look at a real pay stub (yours, or a parent's with permission). Write down gross pay, net pay, and the biggest deduction. What surprised you?

levels.title: Taxes Without the Panic
levels.summary: Standard deduction, how tax brackets really work, and why a raise never hurts.

steps.title: The standard deduction
steps.body:
You do not pay income tax on every dollar. The **standard deduction** is an amount of income that is not taxed at all.

For 2026, a single person gets a **$16,100** standard deduction. It goes up a little most years.

So if your part-time job pays $12,000 in 2026, you likely owe **no federal income tax**. Any federal income tax that was withheld comes back as a refund when you file.
steps.tip: If you earned under the standard deduction this year but federal tax was taken from your checks, put "file a tax return" on your calendar for February so you get that money back.

steps.prompt: In 2026 you earn $9,000 from a summer job and a part-time job. $300 of federal income tax was withheld. What most likely happens when you file?
options: You owe more tax on top of the $300
You get most or all of the $300 back as a refund
Nothing, because teens do not pay taxes
You lose the $300, since it was already sent to the IRS
feedback: Your income is below the $16,100 standard deduction, so you likely owe no federal income tax.
Right. Income under the standard deduction usually means no federal income tax, so withholding comes back.
Age does not matter to the IRS. Teens with income can owe tax; this one just earned under the line.
Withholding is a prepayment. If you owed less, the extra is refunded, but only if you file.
steps.hint: Compare $9,000 to the 2026 standard deduction from the last step.
steps.explain: $9,000 is under the $16,100 standard deduction, so no federal income tax is likely owed. Filing gets the withheld $300 back. (Social Security and Medicare tax is not refunded.)

steps.title: Tax brackets: stairs, not a cliff
steps.body:
US income tax uses **brackets**: rates that rise in steps. Think of filling buckets.

Your first taxable dollars fill the 10% bucket. Once it is full, the next dollars go into the 12% bucket, and so on.

> Only the dollars **above** each line are taxed at the higher rate. The dollars below it keep their lower rate.

So moving into a higher bracket only raises the tax on the extra dollars, not on everything you earn.
steps.tip: When someone says "I do not want overtime, it will bump me into a higher bracket," you can tell them: only the extra dollars get the higher rate, so you still keep most of them.

steps.prompt: If a raise moves you into a higher tax bracket, your take-home pay can go down.
steps.hint: Which dollars get the higher rate: all of them, or only the ones above the line?
steps.explain: The higher rate only applies to dollars above the bracket line. You still keep most of every extra dollar, so a raise always increases take-home pay from tax alone.

steps.prompt: Jordan's taxable income rises just past the line between the 12% bracket and the 22% bracket. Which statement is true?
options: All of Jordan's income is now taxed at 22%
Only the dollars above the line are taxed at 22%
Jordan should turn down extra hours to stay at 12%
Jordan's whole tax bill jumps by 10%
feedback: This is the most common tax myth. The lower buckets keep their lower rates.
Right. Only the dollars past the line land in the 22% bucket.
Turning down hours would lose money. Even at 22%, Jordan keeps 78 cents of each extra dollar before other taxes.
The rate change only hits the few dollars above the line.
steps.hint: Picture buckets: does pouring more water in change what is already in the lower buckets?
steps.explain: Brackets are marginal: each rate applies only to the slice of income inside that bracket.

steps.title: Two kinds of tax on your pay
steps.body:
**Income tax** (federal, and state in most states) depends on how much you earn. The standard deduction and brackets apply to it.

**Social Security and Medicare** tax is a flat 7.65% for employees, starting with your first dollar. There is no standard deduction for it, and you do not get it back as a refund. It funds benefits you can use later in life.

That is why even a tiny paycheck shows some tax.
steps.tip: Look up whether your state has an income tax (search "[your state] income tax" on your state's official .gov site) so you know what to expect on your pay stub.

source.label: IRS: Topic 751, Social Security and Medicare tax rates

steps.prompt: Which of these are true for a teen with a $10,000-a-year job in 2026? Select all that apply.
options: Social Security and Medicare tax comes out of each check
They likely owe no federal income tax
Filing a return can get back federal income tax that was withheld
Social Security and Medicare tax is refunded if income is low
steps.explain: The 7.65% Social Security and Medicare tax applies from the first dollar and is not refunded. Federal income tax on $10,000 is likely zero because of the $16,100 standard deduction, so filing returns any that was withheld.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- The 2026 standard deduction (single) is **$16,100**: income up to that is not hit by federal income tax.
- Brackets work like buckets. Only dollars above a line get the higher rate.
- A raise or overtime **never** lowers your take-home pay because of brackets.
- Social Security and Medicare (7.65%) come out of every check and are not refunded.
steps.tip: Next time you are offered extra hours, decide based on your time and energy, not bracket fears. Every extra hour still adds to your take-home pay.

levels.title: Filing Your First Tax Return
levels.summary: The W-2, free ways to file, deadlines and tax scams.

steps.title: The W-2: your tax report card
steps.body:
By the end of January, every employer you worked for must give you a **W-2** (for 2026 pay, by **February 1, 2027**). It shows what you earned that year and how much tax was withheld.

You need every W-2 to file. If you had three summer jobs, you need three W-2s.

Moved since then? Your W-2 may get mailed to your old address. Many employers also post it in their online payroll site.
steps.tip: Make a folder (paper or a phone album) called "Taxes" this week, and drop every W-2 and tax form into it as it arrives.

steps.prompt: It is mid-February. You worked two jobs last year but only have one W-2. What should you do?
options: File with the one W-2 and skip the other job
Contact the other employer's payroll or HR and ask for your W-2
Guess the numbers from memory
Wait until next year and file both then
feedback: The IRS gets a copy of every W-2. Leaving a job off leads to a letter and a bill later.
Right. Ask payroll, and check their online portal. They may have an old address for you.
Guessed numbers will not match what the employer reported to the IRS.
Each year's return is due that spring. Filing late can mean penalties if you owe.
steps.explain: Employers send the IRS a copy of your W-2, so your return must include all of them. Ask the employer first; if that fails, the IRS can help.

steps.title: Free ways to file
steps.body:
You do not need to pay to file a simple return.
- **IRS Free File** (on irs.gov): free brand-name software. The current limit is an income (AGI) of **$95,000** or less, so most first-job earners qualify.
- **VITA**: free in-person help from IRS-certified volunteers, often at libraries and community centers, generally for people earning about **$70,000** or less.

The deadline is usually **April 15**. Filing online with direct deposit is the fastest way to get a refund.
steps.tip: In January, start from irs.gov/freefile (type it yourself, do not click an ad) so you land on the real free version, not a paid upsell.

steps.prompt: Put these tax-filing steps in order (first to last).
items: Collect every W-2 by early February
Go to IRS Free File or a VITA site
Enter your W-2 numbers and check them
Choose direct deposit for any refund
File before the April deadline and save a copy
steps.explain: Gather forms first, use a free tool, enter and double-check numbers, then pick direct deposit and file. Keep a copy: you may need it for a loan or financial aid.

steps.title: Tax scams
steps.body:
Tax season brings scams. Know this:
- The IRS normally contacts you the first time by **mail**.
- It only emails or texts people who signed up for that, and a social media direct message is never the IRS.
- The IRS never asks for payment by **gift card**.
- Threats of arrest over the phone are a scam sign.

A surprise call, text or DM about taxes is almost always a scammer.
steps.tip: If you get a text about an "IRS refund" with a link, do not tap it. Delete it and report it by forwarding the text to 7726 (SPAM).

source.label: IRS: How to know it's the IRS

steps.prompt: You get a call: "This is the IRS. You owe $900 in back taxes. Pay today with gift cards or police will come to your home." What do you do?

options.text: Hang up. Do not pay. Real IRS issues start with a mailed letter.
options.feedback: Right. Gift cards plus threats is a scam every time.

options.text: Pay a smaller amount to buy time while you check.
options.feedback: Any payment tells the scammer you are an easy target. They will call again.

options.text: Give them your Social Security number so they can look up your file.
options.feedback: Now they can file a fake return or open accounts in your name.

options.text: Call back the number they gave you to confirm.
options.feedback: That number goes straight back to the scammer. Use only numbers from irs.gov.

steps.hint: Think about how the real IRS contacts people first, and how it takes payment.
steps.explain: The IRS contacts you by mail first and never asks for gift cards. Urgency plus an odd payment method is the classic scam signal.

steps.prompt: If your income was low and you do not have to file, filing anyway can still be worth it.
steps.explain: If any federal income tax was withheld, the only way to get it back is to file a return. Filing is also good practice for later years.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Gather every W-2 by early February.
- File for free with IRS Free File or a VITA volunteer.
- The usual deadline is April 15. Pick direct deposit for refunds.
- The IRS normally contacts you by mail first and never wants gift cards.
steps.tip: Save a PDF of every tax return you file in one cloud folder. Lenders, landlords and student aid forms often ask for past returns.

units.title: Budget, Save and Bank
units.description: Give every dollar a job, build a cushion, and keep your bank from eating your money in fees.

levels.title: A Budget You'll Actually Keep
levels.summary: The 50/30/20 starting point, yearly bills and tracking without stress.

steps.title: A budget is a plan, not a punishment
steps.body:
A **budget** is a plan for your take-home pay before you spend it.

A simple starting point is **50/30/20**:
- **50% needs**: rent, groceries, phone, gas, insurance.
- **30% wants**: eating out, games, concerts.
- **20% savings and debt**: emergency fund, investing, paying off cards.

Living at home with few bills? Flip it: save much more than 20% while it is easy.
steps.tip: Open your banking app and add up last month's spending in three piles: needs, wants and savings. That is your starting budget.

steps.prompt: Sort each expense into its 50/30/20 group.
pairs: Money moved to your emergency fund
steps.explain: Needs keep your life running. Wants make it fun. Savings protect future you. A $90 phone plan is a need, but the extra $40 for a premium plan is really a want.

steps.title: Pay yourself first
steps.body:
If you save "whatever is left," there is usually nothing left.

**Pay yourself first**: move savings out the day you get paid, before you spend.

Example: Ava earns $600 every two weeks at her café job. The day after payday, $100 moves to savings automatically. She budgets the other $500 and never misses the $100.
steps.tip: Set up an automatic transfer to savings for the day after each payday this week. Start with any amount, even $20.

steps.title: Yearly bills, monthly savings
steps.body:
Some bills come once or twice a year: car insurance, car registration, a yearly app subscription, holiday gifts.

They feel like emergencies, but they are not. You knew they were coming.

The fix: divide the yearly cost by 12 and save that much each month. When the bill arrives, the money is waiting.
steps.tip: List every bill you pay once or twice a year. Add them up, divide by 12, and set up a monthly transfer for that amount.

steps.prompt: Your car insurance costs $1,200 a year, paid all at once in June. How much should you set aside each month so the money is ready?
steps.hint: There are 12 months in a year. Split the yearly cost evenly across them.
steps.explain: $1,200 / 12 months = **$100 a month**. Save $100 each month and June's bill is already covered.

steps.prompt: Two weeks after payday, you are $60 over your eating-out budget. A friend invites you to a $40 dinner. What is the best move?

options.text: Suggest a cheaper plan, or move $40 from another want (like your games budget) if you really want to go.
options.feedback: Right. A budget bends: you can trade between wants without touching needs or savings.

options.text: Go and put it on a credit card you cannot pay off this month.
options.feedback: Now dinner may cost more than $40 once interest is added.

options.text: Give up on budgeting. It clearly does not work for you.
options.feedback: Going over once is normal. Adjusting is the skill, not being perfect.

options.text: Take the $40 from your rent money and hope it works out.
options.feedback: Needs come first. Short rent leads to late fees or worse.

steps.hint: Which money can you move without hurting a need or your savings?
steps.explain: Good budgets are flexible. Move money between wants, protect needs and savings, and avoid debt for fun.

steps.title: Track without the stress
steps.body:
You do not need to log every coffee forever.

Try a **weekly money check-in**: 10 minutes, same day each week.
- Look at what you spent.
- Compare it to your plan.
- Adjust next week.

Your bank app probably sorts spending into categories already. Many people check in on Sunday night.
steps.tip: Set a repeating 10-minute phone reminder called "Money check-in" for the same evening every week.

steps.prompt: Which budget is most likely to last?
options: Tracking every purchase in a detailed spreadsheet every day
Spending no money on any wants at all
Auto-saving on payday plus a 10-minute weekly check-in
Checking your balance only when your card gets declined
feedback: It can work, but most people burn out within weeks.
Too strict. People who ban all fun usually quit and overspend.
Right. Automation does the hard part, and a short check-in keeps you on track.
By then you may have paid overdraft fees.
steps.explain: The best budget is one you keep. Automate savings and keep tracking light.

steps.prompt: Write your first simple budget: monthly take-home pay, then how much goes to needs, wants and savings.

levels.title: Your Emergency Fund
levels.summary: How much cushion you need, where to keep it and when to use it.

steps.title: Why a cushion matters
steps.body:
Cars break. Phones crack. Shifts get cut. In a 2025 Federal Reserve survey, only **63%** of US adults said they would pay a surprise $400 bill with cash or savings. The rest would have to borrow, sell something, or could not pay.

An **emergency fund** is money set aside only for surprises. Without it, a $500 car repair goes on a credit card or a bad loan and turns into debt.

Step one: a **starter fund of $500-$1,000**. That covers most small emergencies.

Step two: build to **3 months of needs** (rent, food, phone, transportation).
steps.tip: Open a separate savings account named "Emergency Fund" this week, so the money is not mixed with spending money.

source.label: Federal Reserve: Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025

steps.prompt: Which of these is a real emergency fund expense?
options: A great sale on headphones
A $400 car repair you need to get to work
Concert tickets that will sell out
A friend's birthday trip
feedback: A sale is a want, even a good one.
Right. It is unexpected, necessary and urgent.
Fun, but not an emergency. Save for it in a separate goal.
Plan and save for trips separately.
steps.explain: Ask three questions: Is it unexpected? Is it necessary? Is it urgent? An emergency is all three.

steps.title: How big should it be?
steps.body:
A common guideline is **3 to 6 months of needs**, not of all spending. Start with 3. Leave out wants: in a real crisis you would cut them.

Example: Marcus shares an apartment. His rent share, groceries, phone, gas and insurance add up to $1,500 a month. His 3-month goal is the amount that covers 3 of those months.

If your income changes a lot (tips, gig work), aim for 6 months.
steps.tip: Add up your monthly needs only (rent, food, phone, transport, insurance). Write the number on a sticky note: it is the base for your emergency fund goal.

steps.prompt: Your needs cost $1,500 a month. How much is a 3-month emergency fund?
steps.hint: Multiply one month of needs by the number of months.
steps.explain: $1,500 x 3 = **$4,500**. Start with a $500-$1,000 starter fund, then grow toward $4,500.

steps.title: Where to keep it
steps.body:
Keep your emergency fund:
- **Separate** from checking, so you do not spend it by accident.
- **Safe**: in a bank account insured by the FDIC (or NCUA at a credit union), not in stocks that can drop right when you need cash.
- **Earning interest**: a **high-yield savings account** (HYSA) pays much more interest than a typical big-bank savings account.

You should be able to move it to checking in a day or two.
steps.tip: Compare the interest rate on your savings account with two online high-yield savings accounts. If yours pays almost nothing, move your emergency fund.

steps.prompt: You have $1,000 saved. Your laptop for school dies and a basic replacement costs $450. What do you do?

options.text: Use the emergency fund, then rebuild it with extra savings over the next few months.
options.feedback: Right. This is exactly what the fund is for. Refill it afterward.

options.text: Put it on a credit card and keep the fund untouched.
options.feedback: If you cannot pay the card in full, interest makes the laptop cost more. The fund exists so you do not need debt.

options.text: Use a buy now, pay later plan so your savings look bigger.
options.feedback: That adds a debt to protect savings meant for this. Missed payments can bring late fees.

options.text: Go without a laptop until you save a separate $450.
options.feedback: You need it for school now. Waiting could hurt your grades.

steps.explain: An emergency fund only works if you use it for emergencies. Spend it, then refill it.

steps.prompt: Put these money steps in a smart order for someone starting from zero (first to last).
items: Save a $500-$1,000 starter emergency fund
Get any employer 401(k) match
Pay off high-interest credit card debt
Build the emergency fund to 3 months of needs
Invest more for the long term
steps.hint: Start with the cushion that keeps small problems from becoming debt. Free money comes early too.
steps.explain: A small cushion first stops new debt. The employer match is an instant 50-100% return. High-interest debt is next, then the full fund, then long-term investing.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Start with $500-$1,000, then build to 3 months of needs.
- Keep it separate, insured, and in a high-yield savings account.
- Use it for unexpected, necessary, urgent costs, then refill it.
steps.tip: Set an automatic transfer of a fixed amount, like $25 every payday, into your emergency fund until it hits your goal.

levels.title: Pick a Bank and Dodge Fees
levels.summary: Checking vs savings, choosing an account and avoiding overdraft fees.

steps.title: Checking vs savings
steps.body:
**Checking account**: for everyday money. Your paycheck lands here, and your debit card and bills come out of it.

**Savings account**: for money you are not spending right now. It earns interest.

Most people need both: checking for spending, savings for goals and emergencies.

> Deposits at an FDIC-insured bank are protected up to **$250,000** per person, per bank, for each type of account ownership (like single or joint) if the bank fails.
steps.tip: Look for the FDIC (bank) or NCUA (credit union) logo on your bank's website or app before you open an account.

steps.title: What to look for
steps.body:
A good first checking account has:
- **No monthly fee** (or one that is easy to avoid)
- **No minimum balance**
- **Free ATMs** near you, or ATM fee refunds
- A good **app** with alerts

Options: big banks, **credit unions** (member-owned, often lower fees), and online banks. Many offer free student accounts.
steps.tip: Before opening an account, search for its "fee schedule" and read the monthly fee, overdraft fee and ATM fee lines.

steps.prompt: Bank A charges a $12 monthly maintenance fee. Bank B is free. How much more does Bank A cost over a full year?
steps.hint: Multiply the monthly fee by the number of months in a year.
steps.explain: $12 x 12 months = **$144 a year** for nothing. Pick the free account, or meet the waiver rule (like direct deposit) every month.

steps.title: Overdraft: the costly mistake
steps.body:
An **overdraft** happens when you spend more than is in your checking account. The bank may cover it, then charge a fee. The average overdraft fee was about **$27 in 2025**.

So a $5 coffee with $3 in your account can cost $32.

Ways to avoid it:
- **Turn off** (or never opt in to) overdraft coverage for debit cards, so the card is just declined.
- Turn on **low-balance alerts**.
- Link savings as a backup.
steps.tip: Turn on low-balance alerts in your bank app at $100, so you get a warning before you overdraw.

steps.prompt: You have $40 in checking. Your $55 phone bill autopays tomorrow and payday is in three days. What do you do?

options.text: Move money from savings today, or call the phone company to change the date.
options.feedback: Right. A quick transfer or a new due date avoids a fee.

options.text: Do nothing. The bank will cover it.
options.feedback: It may, and charge you an overdraft fee. Or the payment fails and the phone company adds a late fee.

options.text: Withdraw the $40 in cash so the account is empty.
options.feedback: The autopay still runs and overdraws the account.

options.text: Cancel the phone plan.
options.feedback: That is drastic. This is a timing problem, not a spending problem.

steps.hint: The problem is timing: the bill comes before your paycheck. How can you fix the timing or the balance?
steps.explain: Most overdrafts are timing problems. Match bill due dates to payday and keep a small buffer in checking.

steps.prompt: Which habits help you avoid bank fees? Select all that apply.
options: Turning off debit card overdraft coverage
Using your own bank's ATMs
Turning on low-balance alerts
Checking your balance only once a month
steps.explain: Turning off overdraft, using in-network ATMs and alerts all prevent fees. Checking once a month is too rare to catch problems.

steps.prompt: A debit card spends your own money right away, while a credit card borrows money you pay back later.
steps.explain: Debit pulls from checking now. Credit is a short loan that you should pay off in full each month.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Use checking for spending and savings for goals.
- Choose an account with no monthly fee and no minimum balance.
- Turn off debit overdraft coverage, and turn on low-balance alerts.
- Keep money only in FDIC- or NCUA-insured accounts.
steps.tip: Keep a $100 buffer in checking that you treat as $0. It catches small timing mistakes before they become fees.

units.title: Credit Without the Debt
units.description: Build a strong credit score from zero and use a credit card without ever paying interest.

levels.title: Credit Scores Explained
levels.summary: What a credit score is, what moves it and how to check it for free.

steps.title: What is a credit score?
steps.body:
A **credit score** is a number, usually 300 to 850, that tells lenders how likely you are to pay back money you borrow.

It matters more than you think. Landlords, car lenders, phone companies and some employers check credit. A good score can mean a cheaper car loan and an easier time renting your first apartment.

Your score comes from your **credit report**: a record of your loans, cards and payments.
steps.tip: Get your free credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com (type the address yourself). It is the official free site, and you can check weekly.

source.label: CFPB: What is a credit score?

steps.title: What moves your score
steps.body:
For FICO, the most common score:
- **Payment history (35%)**: do you pay on time?
- **Amounts owed (30%)**: how much of your card limits you are using.
- **Length of history (15%)**: how long your accounts have been open.
- **New credit (10%)**: recent applications.
- **Credit mix (10%)**: different types of credit.

The big two are **paying on time** and **using little of your limit**.
steps.tip: Set every card and loan to autopay at least the minimum, so one forgotten due date can never become a late payment on your report.

source.label: myFICO: What's in my FICO Scores?

steps.prompt: Which single habit helps your credit score the most?
options: Checking your own score often
Paying every bill on time
Having lots of different credit cards
Earning a higher salary
feedback: Checking your own score does not change it at all, good or bad.
Right. Payment history is the biggest factor, about 35% of a FICO score.
Opening many cards can lower your score for a while and is harder to manage.
Income is not part of your credit score.
steps.explain: Payment history is the largest factor. A payment 30 or more days late can stay on your report for up to seven years.

steps.title: Utilization: use a little, not a lot
steps.body:
**Credit utilization** is how much of your credit limit you are using. Your **credit limit** is the most a card lets you borrow.

Using a lot of your limit looks risky to lenders, even if you pay in full.

Rules of thumb:
- Keep it **under 30%**.
- **Under 10%** is even better.

If your limit is $1,000, keeping the balance under $300 (better: under $100) helps your score.
steps.tip: Look up your card's credit limit in the app today and write down 30% of it. Try to keep the statement balance under that number.

source.label: Experian: What is a credit utilization rate?

steps.prompt: Your first credit card has a $500 limit. How much is 30% of your limit, the most you want to have showing on your statement?
steps.hint: 30% means 30 out of every 100. Find 10% of $500 first, then multiply by 3.
steps.explain: 10% of $500 is $50. 30% is 3 x $50 = **$150**. Keeping the balance under $50 (10%) is even better.

steps.prompt: Checking your own credit score or report lowers your score.
steps.explain: Checking your own credit is a "soft inquiry" and has no effect. Only applications for new credit ("hard inquiries") can lower it a little for a short time.

steps.prompt: Match each credit term to its meaning.
pairs: The record of your loans, cards and payment history
The most a card lets you borrow
The share of your limit you are using
steps.explain: Your report is the data, your score is the summary. Limit and utilization are about how much you borrow compared to what you could.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Your score tells lenders, landlords and phone companies how risky you are.
- Pay on time, every time: it is the biggest factor.
- Keep utilization under 30%, under 10% is better.
- Checking your own credit is free and never hurts it.
steps.tip: Put a reminder on your calendar every 4 months to check one of your three credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com for accounts you do not recognize.

source.label: CFPB: Does requesting my credit report hurt my score?

levels.title: Build Credit From Zero
levels.summary: Secured cards, authorized users and credit-builder steps that are safe.

steps.title: The no-credit catch
steps.body:
To get credit you need a credit history. To get a history you need credit. Frustrating!

The good news: there are safe on-ramps made for beginners. You do not need debt to build credit. You need an account that reports on-time payments.

Also know: under federal law, if you are **under 21** you need your own income (or a co-signer) to get a credit card.
steps.tip: If you are under 21 and have a job, write down your yearly income before applying. Card applications ask for it, and it must be your own income.

steps.title: Safe ways to start
steps.body:
- **Authorized user**: a parent adds you to their card. Their on-time history can show up on your report. Only do this if they always pay on time and keep a low balance.
- **Secured credit card**: you put down a deposit, like $200, and that becomes your limit. Use it like a normal card.
- **Student card**: a beginner card from your bank or credit union with a low limit.

All three build a history when used carefully.
steps.tip: Ask your bank or credit union this week whether it offers a secured card or student card, and whether it reports to all three credit bureaus.

steps.prompt: Emma is 19, has a part-time job and no credit history. Which first step is safest?
options: Apply for five store cards to get approved somewhere
Open a secured card, use it for one small bill and pay it in full
Take out a personal loan to show she can make payments
Wait until she is 25 to think about credit
feedback: Many applications at once means several hard inquiries, and store cards often have very high interest.
Right. A small, regular charge paid in full builds history with no interest.
Borrowing money you do not need just to build credit costs you interest.
Starting early gives her a longer history, which helps her score.
steps.hint: Look for the option that builds a history without paying interest.
steps.explain: A secured or student card with one small recurring bill, paid in full by autopay, builds credit at no cost.

steps.title: The set-and-forget method
steps.body:
Here is a simple way to build credit with almost no risk:
1. Put **one small bill** on the card, like a $15 streaming plan.
2. Set **autopay for the full statement balance**.
3. Do not use the card for anything else at first.

Every month you get an on-time payment on your report. Your utilization stays low. You never pay interest.
steps.tip: Move one small monthly subscription onto your credit card and turn on autopay for the full statement balance.

steps.prompt: Put these credit-building steps in order (first to last).
items: Open a secured or student card
Put one small monthly bill on it
Turn on autopay for the full statement balance
Check your credit report after a few months
Ask about upgrading to a regular card after about a year
steps.explain: Open the card, add one small bill, automate full payment, then verify your report. Many secured cards can upgrade and return your deposit after months of on-time payments.

steps.prompt: Your aunt offers to add you as an authorized user on her card. She often pays late and the card is nearly maxed out. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her and say no. Her late payments and high balance could hurt your report.
options.feedback: Right. Authorized user status can copy bad history as well as good.

options.text: Say yes. Any credit history is better than none.
options.feedback: Her late payments and high utilization may show on your report and pull your score down.

options.text: Say yes and plan to pay her bill for her.
options.feedback: That is your money paying her debt, and it does not fix the history already there.

steps.hint: Being an authorized user can copy that account's history to your report. Is this history you want?
steps.explain: Only become an authorized user on an account with a long record of on-time payments and a low balance.

steps.prompt: You must carry a balance and pay some interest to build credit.
steps.explain: This is a myth. Paying the full statement balance on time builds credit just as well and costs nothing.

steps.title: Protect your credit: freeze it
steps.body:
A **credit freeze** blocks new lenders from seeing your report. That means a thief cannot open accounts in your name.

It is **free** at all three credit bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. It does not hurt your score. You can lift it in minutes when you apply for a card or loan.

Young people's credit is often stolen because nobody is watching it.
steps.tip: Freeze your credit for free at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion this week, and save the logins or PINs in a password manager.

steps.prompt: Which credit-building path fits you best right now (authorized user, secured card, student card, or wait)? What is the one small bill you would put on it?

levels.title: Use a Credit Card Without Debt
levels.summary: APR, the grace period, the minimum-payment trap and rewards.

steps.title: APR and the grace period
steps.body:
**APR** (annual percentage rate) is the yearly interest rate on a loan or card. Credit card APRs are high: in the third quarter of 2026, the average APR on cards that were charged interest was about **22%** (Federal Reserve).

But there is a way to pay zero interest: the **grace period**. If you pay the **full statement balance** by the due date every month, you usually pay no interest on purchases.

> Treat a credit card like a debit card: only buy what you already have the cash for.
steps.tip: Set your credit card autopay to "statement balance" (not "minimum") today, so you never pay interest on purchases.

steps.title: Statement balance vs current balance
steps.body:
Your card shows two numbers:
- **Statement balance**: what you owed when the last monthly bill was made. Pay this in full to avoid interest.
- **Current balance**: everything so far, including new purchases since the statement.

The **minimum payment** is the smallest amount that avoids a late fee. Paying only the minimum means you are charged interest on the rest.
steps.tip: Open your card app and find the words "statement balance" and "due date." Add the due date to your phone calendar with a 3-day reminder.

steps.prompt: Your statement balance is $300. The minimum payment is $35. What should you pay to avoid interest?
options: Nothing until next month
feedback: That avoids a late fee, but the other $265 starts charging interest.
Paying half still leaves $150 charging interest.
Right. Paying the full statement balance keeps your grace period, so there is no interest.
Missing the due date brings a late fee, interest, and possibly a late mark on your credit report.
steps.hint: Which payment keeps the grace period: the minimum or the whole statement balance?
steps.explain: Pay the full statement balance by the due date and you pay no interest on purchases.

steps.title: The minimum-payment trap
steps.body:
Card companies set the minimum payment low on purpose. If you only pay the minimum, a balance can take **years** to pay off, and you pay much more in interest than you borrowed.

Your statement is required to show how long it would take to pay off the balance with only minimum payments. Read it once: it is a wake-up call.

> If you cannot pay in full, stop using the card and pay as much as you can every month.
steps.tip: Find the "minimum payment warning" box on your next card statement and read how many years minimum payments would take.

source.label: CFPB: The minimum payment warning on your bill

steps.prompt: You owe $800 on a card at 24% APR after an expensive month. You have $250 this month for the card. What is your plan?

options.text: Stop using the card, pay $250 now and as much as possible each month until it is gone.
options.feedback: Right. No new charges plus big payments gets you out fast with the least interest.

options.text: Pay the minimum and keep $200 for fun. You can catch up later.
options.feedback: At 24% APR, the balance barely shrinks and interest piles up.

options.text: Keep using the card for daily spending and pay $250.
options.feedback: New charges can cancel out your payment, so the balance never shrinks.

options.text: Skip this month's payment and pay it all next month.
options.feedback: A missed payment brings a late fee and, after 30 days, a mark on your credit report.

steps.hint: Two things shrink a balance fastest: no new charges and the biggest payment you can manage.
steps.explain: Get out of card debt by freezing new spending and paying well over the minimum every month.

steps.prompt: Getting cash from an ATM with your credit card (a cash advance) works the same as a normal purchase.
steps.explain: Cash advances usually have a fee, a higher APR and no grace period: interest starts the same day. Use your debit card for cash.

steps.title: Rewards: a bonus, not a reason
steps.body:
Many cards give **cash back** or points, like 1-2% of what you spend.

Rewards only help if you pay in full. If you carry a balance at over 20% APR, 2% cash back is wiped out many times over.

Also watch for **annual fees**. A first card should usually have **no annual fee**.
steps.tip: If you are choosing your first card, filter for "no annual fee" first, then compare rewards.

steps.prompt: Which habits let you use a credit card with no interest and good credit? Select all that apply.
options: Autopay the full statement balance
Keep the balance under 30% of your limit
Only charge what you already have cash for
Pay the minimum and invest the rest
steps.hint: Interest costs over 20% a year. Can investing reliably beat that?
steps.explain: Paying in full, keeping utilization low and only spending cash you have keeps a card free and helpful. Card interest is far higher than you can count on earning by investing.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- APR is the yearly interest rate. Card APRs are often over 20%.
- Pay the **full statement balance** every month and you pay no interest on purchases.
- The minimum payment is a trap. Never plan around it.
- No cash advances. No annual fee on a first card.
steps.tip: Before any credit card purchase this week, check that the same amount is sitting in your checking account. If not, do not buy it yet.

units.title: Protect and Grow Your Money
units.description: Dodge scams and bad loans, then let time and simple investing grow your money.

levels.title: Spot Scams and Bad Loans
levels.summary: Payday loans, buy now pay later traps and the red flags of a scam.

steps.title: Payday loans: fast cash, huge cost
steps.body:
A **payday loan** is a small, short loan, usually due on your next payday. A common fee is **$15 for every $100** you borrow for two weeks.

That sounds small, but as an APR it is **almost 400%**. Compare that with about 22% for an average credit card.

The trap: many people cannot repay in two weeks, so they pay another fee to roll it over. And again.
steps.tip: If you are short on cash before payday, ask your employer about a pay advance or your credit union about a small-dollar loan before you ever walk into a payday lender.

steps.prompt: A payday lender charges $15 for every $100 you borrow. You borrow $400 for two weeks. What is the fee?
steps.hint: How many $100s are in $400? Each one costs $15.
steps.explain: $400 is 4 hundreds. 4 x $15 = **$60** for just two weeks. Roll it over a few times and the fees can pass the amount you borrowed.

steps.title: Buy now, pay later (BNPL)
steps.body:
**Buy now, pay later** apps (like "pay in 4") split a purchase into a few payments. Many charge no interest if you pay on time.

The traps:
- **Late fees** if a payment fails.
- **Stacking**: four small plans at once feel tiny, but add up fast.
- It makes it easy to buy things you would not pay cash for.

If you would not buy it with cash today, do not split it.
steps.tip: List every buy now, pay later plan you have and its payment dates in one note. If there are more than one, pause new ones until they are paid off.

steps.prompt: Sneakers cost $160. The checkout offers 4 payments of $40, no interest. You have $60 in checking and already have two other pay-in-4 plans. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it for now and save up. You already have two plans and only $60.
options.feedback: Right. Stacking plans on a thin balance is how late fees and overdrafts start.

options.text: Do it. $40 is small.
options.feedback: It is $40 on top of your other two plans, all pulling from $60. One failed payment means fees.

options.text: Do it, and put the payments on a credit card you cannot pay off.
options.feedback: Now there is interest on top of the plan. Two kinds of debt for one pair of shoes.

steps.hint: Add up all the payments coming out of your account, not just this one.
steps.explain: BNPL is a loan. Before you use one, add up every payment you already owe and check your real balance.

steps.title: The red flags of a scam
steps.body:
Most scams share the same signs:
- **Urgency**: "Act now or your account is closed."
- **Odd payment methods**: gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, or payment apps like Zelle or Venmo to a stranger.
- **Too good to be true**: "Earn $500 a day from home."
- **Overpayment**: someone sends a check for too much and asks you to send back the difference. The check bounces later and you lose the money.

Payment app transfers are like cash. Usually you cannot get them back.
steps.tip: Make a family code word this week. If someone calls claiming to be a relative in trouble and asking for money, ask for the code word.

source.label: FTC: How to avoid a scam

steps.prompt: Which are red flags of a scam? Select all that apply.
options: A job pays you by check, then asks you to send some back by gift card
A text says your bank account is locked and gives a link to unlock it
Your bank app shows a low-balance alert you set up
A stranger online asks you to pay a fee to receive a prize
steps.hint: Look for urgency, links you did not ask for, and requests to send money to get money.
steps.explain: Overpayment checks, surprise links and prize fees are classic scams. An alert you set up yourself is normal.

steps.prompt: You get a text from "your bank" saying there is fraud on your account, with a link to verify. What is the safest move?
options: Tap the link and log in quickly to stop the fraud
Reply STOP to the text
Ignore the text and open your bank's app or call the number on your card
Text back your account number so they can check
feedback: The link likely leads to a fake login page that steals your password.
Replying confirms your number is active. Do not engage.
Right. Contact the bank through a channel you already trust.
Never share account details with someone who contacted you.
steps.explain: When in doubt, go to the source yourself: the official app, website or the number on the back of your card.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Payday loans cost about $15 per $100 for two weeks, almost 400% APR. Avoid them.
- Treat buy now, pay later as debt, and never stack plans.
- Urgency, gift cards and "send back the difference" mean scam.
- Contact companies through their app or the number on your card, never through a link sent to you.
steps.tip: If you are scammed, report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and call your bank right away. Speed raises the chance of stopping a payment.

levels.title: Free Money: Match and Roth IRA
levels.summary: Get your employer's 401(k) match and open a Roth IRA with your first job.

steps.title: The employer match
steps.body:
A **401(k)** is a retirement savings account you get through work. Money comes straight out of your paycheck.

Many employers offer a **match**: they add money when you do. Example: "We match 100% of what you put in, up to 4% of your pay." Put in 4%, and they add another 4%.

That is an instant 100% return. Nothing else gives you that.
steps.tip: Ask HR or check your benefits site this week: "Do you offer a 401(k) match, and what percent do I need to put in to get all of it?"

steps.prompt: You earn $30,000 a year. Your employer matches 100% of your 401(k) savings, up to 4% of your pay. If you save 4%, how much free money does your employer add in a year?
steps.hint: Find 4% of $30,000. Try 1% first (divide by 100), then multiply by 4.
steps.explain: 1% of $30,000 = $300. 4% = 4 x $300 = **$1,200** a year from your employer, on top of your own $1,200.

steps.prompt: Your employer matches up to 4%. You are only putting in 2%. What are you doing?
options: Saving the right amount
Leaving part of the free match on the table
Paying a penalty
Getting the full match anyway
feedback: You could be getting twice as much from your employer.
Right. The match only follows your money, so at 2% you only get 2% added.
There is no penalty. You just miss out on free money.
The match only matches what you put in.
steps.explain: Always put in at least enough to get the full match. It is part of your pay.

steps.title: Vesting: when the match is really yours
steps.body:
**Vesting** is when the employer's match becomes fully yours to keep.

Your own contributions are always 100% yours. But some employers make you stay a while before their match is yours. By law, the match must be fully yours after at most **3 years** (all at once) or **6 years** (a bit more each year). Leave earlier and you may lose some of it.

It is still worth getting the match. Just know your vesting schedule before you switch jobs.
steps.tip: Look up your 401(k) vesting schedule in your benefits portal and note the date your match becomes fully yours.

steps.title: The Roth IRA
steps.body:
An **IRA** is a retirement account you open yourself, at a brokerage like Fidelity, Schwab or Vanguard.

A **Roth IRA** is the best fit for most young workers:
- You put in money you already paid tax on.
- It grows **tax-free**, and withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
- You can take out what you **put in** (not the growth) any time without tax or penalty.

For 2026 the limit is **$7,500** a year, and you can only put in as much as you earned from work.
steps.tip: If you have a job, open a Roth IRA this month at a large brokerage. If you are under 18, ask a parent to open a custodial Roth IRA with you.

steps.prompt: A 17-year-old who earned $3,000 at a summer job can put up to $3,000 into a custodial Roth IRA in 2026.
steps.hint: The yearly limit is $7,500, but there is a second limit tied to work income. Which one is smaller here?
steps.explain: You can put in your earned income or the $7,500 limit (2026), whichever is less. Here that is $3,000. Minors need an adult to open a custodial account.

steps.title: Opening the account is not investing
steps.body:
Here is a common mistake: you put money in a Roth IRA, and it just sits there as cash. It does not grow.

After you deposit, you must **choose an investment** inside the account, like an index fund (next lesson).

The same goes for a 401(k): check that your money is in a fund, not a cash option.
steps.tip: Log in to any retirement account you have and check what your money is invested in. If it says cash or money market, pick a fund.

steps.prompt: Put these first-job retirement steps in a smart order (first to last).
items: Find out if your employer offers a 401(k) match
Put in at least enough to get the full match
Open a Roth IRA
Choose an investment inside each account
Raise your savings rate a little each time you get a raise
steps.explain: Get the free match first, add a Roth IRA, make sure the money is invested, then save more as your pay grows.

steps.prompt: What is your next retirement step: asking about a match, opening a Roth IRA, or choosing a fund? When will you do it?

levels.title: Index Funds and the Power of Time
levels.summary: Why starting early wins, the rule of 72 and simple low-cost investing.

steps.title: Compound growth
steps.body:
**Compound growth** means your money earns returns, and then those returns earn returns too. Like a snowball rolling downhill, it grows faster the longer it rolls.

The biggest ingredient is not how much you invest. It is **time**.

Money invested at 20 has decades more to grow than money invested at 35. That is why starting small, now, beats starting big, later.
steps.tip: Start investing something this month, even $25. Getting the habit and the time on your side matters more than the amount.

steps.prompt: Maya invests $100 a month from age 20 to 30, then stops. Jake invests $100 a month from age 30 to 60. Both earn the same 8% a year. Who most likely has more at 60?
options: Jake, because he invested three times as much
Maya, because her money had 10 extra years to grow
They end up exactly the same
Nobody can tell from this
feedback: Jake put in $36,000 to Maya's $12,000, but his money had less time to grow.
Right. Maya ends up with more, even though she invested only a third as much.
The timing makes a big difference, so they are not the same.
With the same return, the earlier money has more time to compound.
steps.hint: Whose first dollar had longer to snowball?
steps.explain: At 8% a year (not guaranteed), Maya ends with roughly $200,000 and Jake roughly $150,000. Her early money compounded for 30 more years. Time is the superpower.

steps.title: The rule of 72
steps.body:
Want a quick way to see how fast money grows? Use the **rule of 72**:

> 72 divided by the yearly growth rate = about how many years to double.

At 6% a year, money doubles in about 12 years (72 / 6). At 9%, about 8 years.

It works backward too: at a 24% credit card APR, a debt you ignore doubles in about 3 years.
steps.tip: Look up the APR on any debt you have and divide 72 by it. That is roughly how many years it takes for an unpaid balance to double.

steps.prompt: Using the rule of 72, if your investment grows 8% a year, about how many years until it doubles?
steps.hint: Divide 72 by the yearly growth rate.
steps.explain: 72 / 8 = **9 years**. So $1,000 could become about $2,000 in 9 years, and about $4,000 in 18 years, if it keeps growing 8% a year (not guaranteed).

steps.title: Index funds: buy the whole basket
steps.body:
Picking single stocks is risky: one company can crash.

An **index fund** buys a small piece of hundreds or thousands of companies at once. An **S&P 500 fund** holds about 500 large US companies. A **total market fund** holds even more.

Why beginners love them:
- Instant **diversification** (spreading risk).
- Very **low fees**.
- No need to pick winners.
steps.tip: In your Roth IRA or 401(k), look for a broad index fund (S&P 500, total market, or a target-date fund) and check its expense ratio.

steps.title: Fees: small percents, big money
steps.body:
The **expense ratio** is the yearly fee a fund charges, as a percent of your money.

In 2025, the average stock index ETF charged **0.14%** a year, and the average stock mutual fund **0.40%** (ICI). Many broad index funds charge even less. Some actively managed funds charge several times more.

A fee is taken every year for decades, so a small difference grows into a lot of lost money.
steps.tip: Look up the expense ratio of every fund you own. If one is far above 0.20%, compare it with a broad index fund.

source.label: ICI: Mutual fund and ETF fees in 2025

steps.title: Expect ups and downs
steps.body:
The stock market does not rise in a straight line. In 2008 the S&P 500 lost about **37%**, and in 2022 about **18%**. Both times it later recovered and went on to new highs.

Long-term investors keep going and do not sell in a panic.

> Only invest money you will not need for at least 5 years. Short-term money stays in savings.
steps.tip: Turn off daily price notifications in your investing app. Check your long-term investments a few times a year, not every day.

steps.prompt: You started investing $50 a month in an index fund. Six months later the market drops 15% and your balance is down. What do you do?

options.text: Keep investing on schedule. You are buying at lower prices, and you have decades.
options.feedback: Right. Drops are normal. Staying in is how long-term investors win.

options.text: Sell everything before it drops more.
options.feedback: Selling locks in the loss. Many of the best days come soon after the worst ones.

options.text: Move it all into one hot stock to win it back fast.
options.feedback: That adds risk right when you are feeling the pain. One stock can drop to zero.

options.text: Stop investing until the news looks better.
options.feedback: Nobody can time the market. Waiting often means missing the recovery.

steps.hint: Think about your time horizon. Do you need this money next month or in 40 years?
steps.explain: For long-term money, drops are temporary sales. Keep investing steadily and do not panic-sell.

steps.prompt: Money you will need for a car down payment in 6 months belongs in an index fund so it can grow.
steps.explain: The market could be down right when you need the money. Short-term goals belong in a high-yield savings account. Invest only money you will not need for 5+ years.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Time is the biggest ingredient: start small, start now.
- Rule of 72: 72 / growth rate = years to double.
- Broad, low-fee index funds are a simple way to invest.
- Expect drops. Keep investing and do not panic-sell.
- Money for the next few years stays in savings.
steps.tip: Set up an automatic monthly investment, even $25, into a broad index fund in your Roth IRA, so investing happens without you having to decide each month.
